  MINUTES
  Regular Meeting
  ALHAMBRA CITY COUNCIL
  Ruth Reese Hall, 101 South First Street
  March 22, 2021
  6:00 p.m.

ROLL CALL: At 6:12 p.m., on Monday, March 22, 2021 the Alhambra City Council met via
video conference.

COUNCIL PRESENT via video conference: LEE, MAZA, MALONEY, ANDRADE-STADLER,
PÉREZ
ABSENT:  NONE

Officials Present physically, via teleconference, and via video conference: City Manager
Binnquist, City Attorney Montes, Assistant City Manager Garcia, Deputy City Manager Tran,
City Clerk Myles, Director of Finance Lieu, Director of Public Works/ Utilities Ray, Director of
Parks and Recreation Macias, Marketing and Communications Specialist Nguyen, Management
Analyst Cuevas, Director of Community Development Castagnola, Fire Chief Phelps, Police
Chief Vu, Director of Human Resources Ko, Deputy Director of Utilities Dolphin, Principal
Planner Lam

FLAG SALUTE:  Mayor Pérez

CITY CLERK REPORT - NOTICE NO. N2M21-34

The City Clerk reported that she duly gave notice of the regular meeting of the City Council
being held pursuant to the order of the Mayor in accordance with Section 54955 and 54956 of
the Government Code of the State of California.

READING OF ORDINANCE TITLES
Government Code Section 36934 requires that all ordinances be read in full prior to City Council
taking action on the ordinance. By listing the ordinance title on the Council agenda, Council may
determine that the title has been read.

Action Taken:  On motion of Ms. LEE, seconded by Mr. MAZA, the City Council
determined that the titles to all ordinances which appeared on this public agenda had been
read, and waived further reading. Hearing no objections, the Mayor so ordered.

CEREMONIAL

1.  PROCLAMATION: WOMEN’S HISTORY MONTH – F2M21-3

  Ratified the action of Mayor Pérez in proclaiming the month of March, 2021 as
  WOMEN’S HISTORY MONTH in Alhambra.

 PRESENTATIONS

2.  DISCUSSION CONCERNING A POSSIBLE ORDINANCE TO RESTRICT SMOKING
  AND THE SALE OF FLAVORED TOBACCO PRODUCTS – F2M21-16

  City Attorney MONTES delivered a staff report. At the request of Mayor Pérez and
  Councilmember Andrade-Stadler, on February 22, 2021 the City Council received a
  presentation on limiting smoking within the City, as well as limiting the sale of flavored
  tobacco products. The Council requested further discussion concerning whether or not
  to adopt any regulations in those subject areas. Mr. MONTES provided some
  background as well as options for the Council, should the Council wish to move forward
  with any such regulation.

  Public Comment:

  1) Adam BRAY-ALI requested clarification regarding the impact of the ordinance on
  smoking outdoors on private property.

  The following people spoke in favor of the proposed ordinance and spoke
  regarding the negative impact of second-hand smoke, tobacco companies
  targeting youth in marketing, and the benefits of a Tobacco Retail License
  program:

  1) Primo Castro, representing the American Cancer Society, also submitted a letter to
  Council which is on file.
  2) Sandra Kwok, a student at Monterey Highlands School and a member of Alhambra
  Unified School District Tobacco Use Prevention Education Student Advocates, also
  submitted a letter to Council which is on file.
  3) Sophie Lin, a student at San Gabriel High School and a member of Alhambra Unified
  School District Tobacco Use Prevention Education Student Advocates, also
  submitted a letter to Council which is on file.
  4) Nicolas Kiet Quach, a student at Alhambra High, a member of Alhambra Unified
  School District Tobacco Use Prevention Education Student Advocates, an intern for
  Mayor Pérez, and a member of the Alhambra Youth Commission, also submitted a
  letter to Council which is on file.
  5) Guadulesa Rivera, representing the Breathe Free Alhambra Coalition, also read
  some of written comments from other Alhambra Unified School District students.
  6) Champ Liudi, a student at Mark Keppel High School, also submitted a letter to
  Council which is on file.
  7) Elizabeth Jacoby, representing the Los Angeles County Tobacco Control and
  Prevention Program
  8) Allyson Vuong, a student at Martha Baldwin Elementary School, also submitted a
  letter which is on file.
  9) Annie Tegan, representing the Campaign for Tobacco Free Kids
  10) Lisa Lu, a student at Stanford University, an alumna of Brightwood and Baldwin
  Middle school, and founder of International Youth Tobacco Control
  11) Gianna Karkafi, a student at San Marino High School and member of the
  International Youth Tobacco Control
  12) Elaina Lee, a student at San Marino High School and member of the International

3-22-21
   Discussion: Council thanked all speakers for their comments and expressed gratitude
  towards the youth for their civic engagement. Council also discussed the negative
  impact of smoking on youth. Council supported the Tobacco Retail Licensing Program.
  Mr. MONTES further clarified points within the staff report regarding additional outdoor
  smoking regulations and the specific points needing Council direction. He further
  clarified points in the staff report regarding Tobacco Retail Licensing and sale of flavored
  tobacco, including considerations for the impact of the ordinance.

  Councilmember ANDRADE-STADLER suggested allowing current businesses time to
  sell or remove any existing tobacco products or amortization period. This was supported
  by Council. Ms. Andrade-Stadler supported adding all outdoor areas mentioned to
  existing ordinance. Councilmember MALONEY discussed the designation of non-public
  buildings and outdoor worksites with Mr. Montes. He supported restrictions on non-
  public buildings and sidewalks, but added that restrictions against outdoor worksites and
  service areas be set by employers and building owners. Councilmembers Lee, Maza,
  and Pérez supported this. Mayor PÉREZ, Mr. MAZA, and Mr. MONTES discussed Mr.
  Bray-Ali’s questions regarding the impact of outdoor smoking on private property. Mr.
  MAZA suggested that the restrictions apply to complexes of more than 6 or 8 units.

  Mayor PÉREZ suggested that the restrictions on public events and enclosed areas be
  set at a 6 feet radius. She supported the Tobacco Retail Licensing Program and that it
  would include a prohibition against coupons and discounts. Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER
  and Mr. MONTES discussed sample language provided by Mr. Castro and the American
  Cancer Society referring to the prohibition of coupons to be included in the ordinance.
  Mr. MALONEY and Mr. MONTES discussed the non-smoking radius used by Public
  Building Standard of 20 feet and the minimum number of units in multi-unit
  developments.

  Action Taken:  City Council directed staff to draft a Tobacco Retail License
  ordinance; expand the scope of the existing Smoking Prohibition Ordinance; and return
  both ordinances for First Reading at a future Council meeting.

3.  ANNUAL BOARDS AND COMMISSIONS APPOINTMENTS – F2M21-31

  City Clerk MYLES delivered a staff report. The terms of office for all members of the
  City’s various Boards and Commission expired on March 22, 2021; therefore, it was
  appropriate for Councilpersons to appoint or reappoint their representatives at this time.
  With the exception of the Youth Commission, each representative may serve for a
  maximum of eight consecutive terms of one year each. Appointments would be effective
  for a period commencing March 22, 2021 and ending March 28, 2022.

  Discussion: The Mayor and each Councilperson announced his/her new
  appointments to the various Boards/Commissions. Councilmember ANDRADE-
  STADLER appointed Maria Jimenez to the Alhambra City Arts & Cultural Events
  Committee; Nora Hernandez to the Design Review Board; Michael Soto to the HCDA
  Advisory Board; Laura Longoria to the Board of Library Trustees; David Soto and Josh
  Moreno to the Parks and Recreation Commission; and appointed Joselyn Cooper,
  Carmen Manuel Jose, and Daniela Andrade to the Youth Commission.

  4
3-22-21
   Councilmember MALONEY appointed Calimay Pham to the Planning Commission; and
  Mike Fong to the Transportation Commission.

  Councilmember MAZA appointed Wing Ho to the Planning Commission.

  Councilmember LEE appointed Ari Gutierrez Arambula to the Environmental Committee.

  Mayor PÉREZ appointed Patti Sanchez to the City Arts & Cultural Events Committee;
  Matthew Rutzen to the Civil Service Commission and Board of Appeals; Jose L.
  Espinoza Jr. to the Design Review Board; Katie Chan to the Environmental Committee;
  Bill Vallejos and Lewis McCammon to the HCDA Citizen Advisory Committee; Maurice
  Norrington and David Nguyen to the Parks and Recreation Commission; Kent Tsujii and
  Chris Olson to the Planning Commission; Kristopher Fortin and Henry Aviles to the
  Transportation Commission; and Maria Romano, Nicholas Quach and Mark Munson to
  the Youth Commission. Ms. Pérez referred to a discussion she had with her Youth
  Commission members regarding the poor attendance of the other commissioners. She
  encouraged Council to reach out to commissioners and reported that an attendance
  report would be provided to Council. She continued to discuss the importance of Youth
  Commissioners and their responsibilities.

  Ms. LEE suggested a stipend or compensation for Commissioners due to the high level
  of work conducted by Planning and Design Review Board Commissioners. She referred
  to other cities which provide a stipend and should Council agree, she requested that
  staff conduct research into the matter. The other Councilmembers refrained from
  comment and without unanimous support the matter was tabled. Mr. MALONEY, Ms.
  PÉREZ, and Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER suggested discussing the matter during other
  planned discussions specific to each commission at future Council meetings. Mr. MAZA
  suggested that Council receive feedback from the current Board and Commission
  members who would be considered for a stipend.

  Action Taken:  The Mayor and each Councilperson announced their new
  appointments to the Civil Service Commission/Board of Appeals, HCDA Citizen Advisory
  Committee, Board of Library Trustees, Parks & Recreation Commission, Planning
  Commission, Design Review Board, Transportation Commission, Youth Commission,
  the Alhambra City Arts & Cultural Events Committee and the Environmental Committee
  with each appointment to be effective for a period commencing March 22, 2021 and
  ending March 28, 2022. Other than announcing the names of all new appointees, no
  action was required as the incumbents for each position were automatically reappointed
  unless otherwise indicated by the appointing Councilmember or in the City Clerk’s March
  22, 2021 staff report on file in the City Clerk’s office.

4.  PRESENTATION ON THE STORMWATER MASTER PLAN – F2M20-21

  Deputy Director of Utilities DOLPHIN delivered a staff report and introduced Brad
  WARDYNSKI, Merrill TAYLOR, and Chad HELMLE representing Craftwater
  Engineering, who delivered a PowerPoint presentation which is on file in the City Clerk’s
  office. The Safe Clean Water (SCW) Program was a multi-benefit stormwater and/or
  urban runoff capture program intended to improve water quality in a manner that
  achieves additional benefits such as increasing water supply and investing in the health
  and well-being of Los Angeles County communities. Funding was available through the

  5
3-22-21
   SCW Regional and Municipal Programs. The Municipal Program would provide a steady
  funding stream for the City; however, 70% of the monies received must be utilized on
  new projects. The Regional Program funds were competitive and must be spent on
  eligible activities relating to multi-benefit stormwater projects, their design, construction,
  land acquisition, operations, maintenance, and programs. In order to comply with the
  SCW Program’s stringent funding requirements, the City was in the process of
  developing a Stormwater Master Plan that would implement cost effective strategies to
  identify potential stormwater projects and prioritize the planning process. Potential
  opportunities were identified and screened by project design engineers to ensure that all
  identified opportunities met basic feasibility considerations. Criteria used in this
  screening process included; topography and the existing storm drain network, patterns
  of imperviousness across the City, geospatial analysis as well as the Engineers’
  professional judgement. A site assessment of every opportunity identified was
  completed to eliminate those that would not likely make it through to design and
  construction phases due to a range of potential site-specific challenges.

  Discussion: Councilmember MALONEY discussed the expenditure plan’s submission
  to the County, Council’s involvement, community engagement, and individual projects
  with Mr. DOLPHIN. Mr. MALONEY further discussed BMPs and multi-benefit projects as
  they related to developing public open space and existing park space with Mr. Dolphin.
  They continued to discuss lack of development of the 710 stub with Mr. HELMLE, due to
  its ownership by CalTrans. Mr. MALONEY suggested that should discussions proceed
  with CalTrans and the County, that the City consider a joint project with Los Angeles
  County Flood Management. Mr. MALONEY and Mr. DOLPHIN continued to discuss a
  potential watershed project at the Alhambra Golf Course.

  Mayor PÉREZ expressed excitement over the plan and the prospect of being one of the
  first Southern California cities to adopt such a plan.

  Action Taken:  City Council received and ordered filed this informational report.

RECESS:  At approximately 8:25 p.m., Mayor Pérez called for a brief recess.

RECONVENE:  The City Council returned and the meeting reconvened at approximately
8:33 p.m.

PÉREZ:  Due to the high volume of public speakers for the next item, the continued public
hearing, Mayor Pérez suggested that public comment would be received until 9:45 p.m., at
which point Council would continue the item to a Special City Council Meeting to be held at a
future date. Council agreed.

CONTINUED PUBLIC HEARING

5.  APPLICATIONS FOR VESTING TENTATIVE TRACT MAP TT 74194, RESIDENTIAL
  PLANNED DEVELOPMENT PERMIT RP-17-7, CONDITIONAL USE PERMIT CU-17-9
  AND DEVELOPMENT AGREEMENT FOR THE DEVELOPMENT OF THE PROPOSED
  VILLAGES AT THE ALHAMBRA PROJECT (PROJECT) WITH 294 NEW, FOR-SALE,
  RESIDENTIAL DWELLING UNITS IN FIVE-STORY STACKED FLAT AND
  TOWNHOME CONFIGURATIONS; 545 NEW RENTAL APARTMENTS IN FIVE-
  STORY STACKED FLAT CONFIGURATIONS; AND UP TO 4,347 TOTAL PARKING
  SPACES TO ACCOMMODATE ALL NEW USES. IT IS EXPECTED THAT IF THE

  6
3-22-21
   PROJECT IS APPROVED THE APPLICANT WILL IMPLEMENT A PARKING
  REDUCTION PURSUANT TO ALHAMBRA MUNICIPAL CODE SECTION 23.52.060.
  THE PROJECT SITE IS LOCATED IN THE PO (PROFESSIONAL OFFICE) ZONE. AN
  ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT REPORT HAS BEEN PREPARED FOR THE PROJECT
  AND WILL ALSO BE CONSIDERED WITH THE PROJECT ALONG WITH A
  POSSIBLE STATEMENT OF OVERRIDING CONSIDERATIONS – F2M17-50, N2M20-
  163

  Mayor PÉREZ clarified to the public that no official deal had been made, nor had
  Councilmembers Andrade-Stadler and Maza indicated how they would vote on the
  matter. She clarified that the this was a proposal and discussed the options open to
  Council decision with City Attorney MONTES. Mr. MONTES clarified that the appointed
  sub-committee would report on their negotiation with the developer and then Staff
  sought direction as to whether Council would like to move forward with revised
  documents for approval at a continued City Council meeting or if Council would like to
  continue negotiations with regard to deal points in the development agreement. He
  stated that in such case, Council would need to provide specific direction to the sub-
  committee for negotiation. He stated that alternatively, Council could also consider
  directing staff to prepare documents to deny the project. Mr. Montes further discussed
  the limitations on denying the project given the zoning permitted for the site.

  Director of Community Development CASTAGNOLA delivered a staff report. This was
  the time and place set by Notice No. N2M20-163 for the City Council to hold a public
  hearing, which public hearing was duly continued from the January 11, 2021 meeting,
  the January 27, 2021 meeting and the February 4, 2021 meeting, to receive a report
  from the designated sub-committee of Councilmembers appointed to represent the
  Council’s concerns with the project and negotiate a compromise for the project
  Development Agreement. At a special meeting on February 4, 2021, the City Council
  considered the application by the Ratkovich Company for the Village at the Alhambra
  project, comprised of a total of 839 residential units, including 294 condominiums and
  545 apartments units. During discussion of the item, the City Council appointed a sub-
  committee of Councilmembers Adele Andrade-Stadler and Ross Maza to represent the
  Council’s concerns with the project and negotiate a compromise for the project
  Development Agreement. The Council sub-committee met on a weekly basis for five
  substantial discussions. At the conclusion of the meetings, the Council sub-committee
  reached an agreed upon number of deal points pursuant to several community benefits.

  Councilmembers ANDRADE-STADLER thanked Megan MOLOUGHNEY, Senior
  Development Manager for The Ratkovich Company and Brian Saenger of the Ratkovich
  Company for their productive meetings. She went on to speak to the benefits of the
  project site and the ways it would add additional housing to meet the City’s RHNA
  numbers, providing homes to potential employees in the city of Alhambra, add to the
  Alhambra campus by providing several amenities. She also thanked Mr. Maza for his
  work and cooperation. She further outlined the items that were discussed such as: the
  Inclusionary Housing Ordinance, the 50-50 moderate income owners and renters, legal
  service assistance for homeless, a density of 700, 4 intersections under LOS, interval or
  paced development, a park at the former Lowe’s site, a park elsewhere in the
  community, a park inside the site itself, pedestrian safety crosswalks, enhancing visibility
  for pedestrians, reinforcing the right-of-way over trucks, vapor mitigation built into the
  design rather than passive, future protection and testing for families, EV program and
  charging stations, electric or lower build, access to impact fees, as well as LOS (Level

  7
3-22-21
   of Service) versus VMT (Vehicle Miles Traveled) and the transition.

  Councilmember MAZA thanked Ms. Andrade-Stadler, the Ratkovich Company, and Mr.
  Castagnola for their work and cooperation during negotiations. He reported on the
  subcommittee’s tour of the potential site. He reported on their meeting with city staff
  regarding the concerns of fellow Councilmembers and the community. He also identified
  topics of discussion such as: affordability, traffic, environmental issues and concerns,
  indemnifying the City of Alhambra from any exposure to future liability from this project,
  pedestrian safety, estimated build time, accessibility for Alhambra residents, community
  room, non-passive vapor barrier, pre and post-construction inspections, community
  needs and compensation to the City of Alhambra such as park space, dog park
  elsewhere in the city, and funds for additional affordable housing.

  Mr. MAZA referred to the staff report which outlined to the City Council those deal points
  and community benefits which included the following:
  1.  Agreed upon Deal Points:
  A. The total number of residential units will be reduced to 775 units
  comprised of:
    230 condominiums for-sale units; and,
    545 rental apartment units, including:
    75 rental apartment affordable units at the Moderate Area Median Income
  level (13.76% of total rental units).

  B. A community benefit payment of $1.5 million to be dispensed at the
  Council’s discretion.

  2.  Additional Community Benefits: Project Density - Following negotiation, the
  total number of units was further reduced to 775 units, resulting in a density of
  20.2 units to the acre; Open Space - While the project is significantly reduced
  from its original residential count, it will maintain the original 16 acres of open
  space and the open space will be accessible to all Alhambra residents; Trees -
  All existing trees currently on the property that may need to be removed for the
  project will be offered to the City for relocation to other locations; Traffic - As a
  result of the reduction of residential units and the State mandate to analyze the
  environmental impact of traffic based on the Vehicle Miles Traveled (VMT)
  methodology, no significant impacts can be identified. However, the Ratkovich
  Company is still committed to providing two new intersections and pedestrian
  improvements; Air Quality - Because of the reduced number of units, air quality
  impacts temporarily resulting from construction will be reduced and The
  Ratkovich Company is currently studying a construction schedule to eliminate all
  temporary air quality significant impacts; and, Soil contamination mitigation –
  following concerns of potential vapor contamination, the Ratkovitch Company
  will: Install a vapor barrier under the Corner Plan residential building; Provide a
  concrete cap under the East Plan parking structure; and, Provide pre-occupancy
  air quality testing on the Corner Plan residential units. In addition, the Ratkovich
  Company will be providing the City with an indemnity for future potential risks.

  Staff sought direction on working with the project applicant to revise the draft
  Development Agreement for further consideration by the City Council.

  8
3-22-21
   Applicant:  Megan MOLOUGHNEY, Senior Development Manager for The Ratkovich
  Company thanked Councilmembers Andrade-Stadler and Maza for their effort during the
  subcommittee meetings. She discussed the background in reducing the density to 775
  units which addressed the concerns of the public, meets the California RHNA level in
  housing, and would be 50% less than the allowable density for the site. She went on to
  report on the discussions about moderate income affordable units, and pointed out that
  the 75 units were still included despite an overall reduction of units and without the use
  of public subsidies. She reported that due to concerns voiced regarding low-income
  housing and suggestions of park space throughout the city, they agreed to make a
  payment to the City which would satisfy all needs and allow Council time to prioritize use
  of funds. She stated that these funds as well as leveraging CDBG funds and available
  grant funding could effectively produce an additional 55-unit affordable project similar to
  current projects on Second and Chapel. Ms. Moloughney reiterated that the intention
  was to empower the Council to decide the best use of funds and allow for time to
  properly allocate and maximize use of the dollars.

  Ms. Moloughney went on to report on the additional community benefits from the project.
  She discussed the VMT study as adopted by the City as well as an independent review
  by the city’s consultant, which concluded there would be no significant traffic impacts
  due to the project. She further discussed concerns of pedestrian safety and stated that
  two new traffic signals and crosswalks would be provided at the intersection of Date and
  Orange as well as Date and Mission. She stated that these would be great
  improvements to the community. Ms. Moloughney next addressed concerns regarding
  soil contamination and referred to Council’s discussions with an Environmental
  Protection Agency representative at the January 11, 2021 Council meeting. She stated
  that the developer agreed to install a vapor barrier under the corner planned building and
  provide pre-occupancy testing for those units. She stated that this would include on-
  going monitoring as deemed by the regulatory agency. Additionally, the East Plan
  parking structure would serve as a concrete cap to prevent any potential or future vapor
  intrusion. She also addressed concerns regarding temporary regional air quality impact
  and stated that the developer was exploring alternative construction schedules to
  eliminate the impact altogether. Ms. Moloughney went on to discuss the desire for more
  greenspace and stated that by code, the project was required to have 10 acres of open
  space but that the developer proposed 16 acres of open green space which would
  include a larger community park in the North Plan area. She pointed out that usually
  greenspace is provided in relation to density, but that there was no reduction in
  greenspace after reducing the project density. She reiterated that the project was
  providing well above what was required by Code with the goal of enhancing and
  complimenting the existing campus and providing additional park space in the City. She
  stated that there would also be an additional 650 trees planted on the 16 acres and that
  the project would meet all local, state, and federal regulations for environmental
  protection. She stated that the Villages would support local small businesses by
  providing more potential near-by customers and would maintain the local farmer’s
  market. Ms. Moloughney summarized by stating that the project would have a reduced
  density from the allowable density, would be a redevelopment of underutilized land to
  build housing during a housing crisis without displacing residents, would provide an
  opportunity for the City to substantially contribute its RHNA goals with multiple levels of
  product and affordability both on-site and potentially off-site, would bring uses together
  to promote walkability and alignment with State VMT goals to reduce traffic, would
  present significant economic benefits to the city and school district.

  9
3-22-21
   Opened the Public Hearing:  Mayor Pérez opened the Public Hearing.

  Public Comment:

  The following people spoke against the project, the developers profiting off of the
  development regardless of the impact on the community, lack of accessibility to
  existing residents to proposed public spaces, and listed concerns with
  insufficient proposals to address project density, traffic impacts, and affordable
  low-income housing:

  1)  Raul Barrera
  2)  Joe Soltero
  3)  Karla Zombro
  4)  Adam Bray-Ali
  5)  Ari G. Arambula
  6)  Lewis McCammon
  7)  Michael Lawrence

  The following people spoke in favor of the project, the strengths of the Ratkovich
  Company and their past successes, the benefits to the local community by
  providing more housing to increase the local economy, allow the City flexibility to
  address specific plans elsewhere in the City, address increased State housing
  mandates, and provide necessary updates to the City:

  1) John Tilley
  2) Sharon Gibbs

PEREZ:  Mayor Perez discussed pausing public comment and continuing the item to
another date. Councilmember LEE and Councilmember MAZA suggested continuing the public
speakers and continuing the written comment to another meeting. Councilmember MALONEY
stated that commenters could choose to hold their comments until the special meeting, but that
if they could not attend, then they should be allowed to speak this evening. Ms. PÉREZ stated
that there were still many other items on the agenda for discussion. Councilmember ANDRADE-
STADLER stated that Council previously discussed pausing the item at 9:45 p.m. and that they
should continue with that decision due to the other items that needed action this evening. City
Clerk MYLES used the “raise hand” option on Zoom to see if there were any objections from the
public to continue comments at the next special meeting. There were no objections from the
public. Council continued to discuss the merits of allowing more public comment at the current
meeting, continuing to a special meeting, and Council’s decision-making process to make a
determination. Mr. MALONEY motioned to continue the item to a special City Council meeting;
which was seconded by Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER. Council continued to discuss the date of the
special meeting and determined it would be held on April 13, 2021 at 6:00 p.m. Ms. LEE
requested that the developer clarify their promotion of the project by stating that a deal had not
yet been reached with the City. Ms. MOLOUGHNEY clarified that the Ratkovich Company used
language that reflected the information provided in the staff report.

  Action Taken:  City Council continued the hearing to a special City Council
  meeting on April 13, 2021 at 6:00 p.m.

6.  NIB: SEWER SYSTEM SMOKE TESTING INSPECTION PROJECT – F2M21-32,
  N2M21-35

  The primary purpose of Smoke Testing inspection is to identify sections of the sanitary
  sewer collection system that have cracks, leaks or faulty connections such as roof
  downspouts, driveway and yard drains, and other types of area drains with direct piped
  connections to sanitary sewer laterals; as well as defective or open cleanouts on private
  property that are located in areas that may collect surface drainage that allow rainwater
  to enter the underground pipe network. Since the sanitary sewer system is only
  designed to handle sewage, the addition of rainwater/storm water causes many
  problems in the collection system. The smoke used for testing of the sewer system is
  odorless, non-toxic and non-staining. Plans and specifications were prepared; staff
  reviewed the plans and found them to be consistent with the City’s standards.

  Discussion:  None.

  Action Taken:  City Council approved the distribution of a Notice Inviting Bids to
  qualified contractors for the Sewer System Smoke Testing Inspection Project with bids
  due no later than 10:30 a.m. on April 8, 2021; and, directed staff to undertake the steps
  necessary to finalize Council’s action.

16.  FIRST READING OF AN ORDINANCE ADDING CHAPTER 6.13 TO THE ALHAMBRA
  MUNICIPAL CODE PERTAINING TO DISPOSABLE FOODWARE ITEMS OPT-IN
  REQUIREMENT FOR RESTAURANTS AND THIRD-PARTY APP-BASED DELIVERY
  PLATFORMS – F2M21-7, O2M21-4783

  At the March 8, 2021 City Council meeting, the City Council directed staff to return with
  an ordinance that would require restaurant patrons utilizing takeout or food delivery
  services to “opt-in” to receiving disposable foodware items (i.e., disposable plates,
  napkins, straws, utensils, etc.). More specifically, the proposed ordinance would require:
  1) That restaurants and other food service providers only provide disposable foodware
  items upon the request of the customer, or in self-serve stations; 2) That third-party, app-
  based delivery platforms include on their platforms an option for customers to

  15
3-22-21
   affirmatively request disposable foodware items; and 3) That City staff work with food
  service providers on a public awareness campaign to make customers aware of the “opt-
  in” program and its environmental benefits.

  Public Comment:  David JUAREZ, representing the California Restaurant
  Association, spoke in support of the ordinance. He requested that mandate which
  required food service establishments and third-party applications include an option for
  customers to request foodware items for delivery or takeout remove the language for
  food service establishments. He stated that this mandate made sense for third party
  applications but would impose extra costs against smaller businesses to update their
  websites and delivery promotional materials. He reasoned that customers would still be
  able to request foodware items at the time they placed their orders for delivery or
  takeout, but that it should not be required for food service establishments to include a
  separate option for customers on their online platforms.

  Public Comment received via email on file in the City Clerk’s office: Melissa
  MICHELSON wrote in support of the ordinance and suggested further ordinances to
  make restaurants more environmentally sustainable.

  Discussion: Mayor PÉREZ referred to Mr. Juarez’s comments and requested that the
  language requiring food service establishments provide online options to request
  disposable foodware options. Councilmember MALONEY and City Attorney MONTES
  discussed the specific requirement as it related to food service establishment’s private
  websites. Mr. MALONEY motioned to remove the requirement, but suggested that as
  part of the outreach to food service establishments the City educate them on how to best
  comply with the ordinance.

  Action Taken: City Council introduced for first reading the following ordinance entitled:
  Ordinance No. O2M21-4783: An Ordinance of the City Council of the
  City of Alhambra Adding Chapter 6.13 to the Alhambra Municipal Code
  pertaining to disposable foodware items opt-in requirement for
  restaurants and third-party app-based delivery platforms
  directed staff to amend language requiring food service establishments provide online
  options to request disposable foodware; and, directed staff to agendize said Ordinance
  for a second reading and possible adoption at the next regular Council meeting.

  Vote:  Moved:  MALONEY  Seconded: ANDRADE-STADLER
  Ayes:  MAZA, LEE, ANDRADE-STADLER, MALONEY, PÉREZ
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE
